seeds.asked: enumerate branches of typical intercostal nerve
seeds.label: A typical intercostal nerve runs in the neurovascular bundle below the vein and artery, and ends as the anterior cutaneous branch
seeds.definition: The typical intercostal nerves are the anterior primary rami of the second to sixth thoracic spinal nerves. Its branches are ganglionic rami communicantes to the sympathetic chain, a collateral branch to the muscles, muscular branches, a lateral cutaneous branch, the terminal anterior cutaneous branch, articular branches and pleural branches. The second nerve's lateral cutaneous branch crosses the axilla to the arm as the intercostobrachial nerve instead of dividing locally.
seeds.objective: List the branches of a typical intercostal nerve.
seeds.pitfall: Forgetting that the nerve is the lowest of the three neurovascular structures (VAN) in the costal groove.
seeds.subject: resp

seeds.asked: summarize relations of mediastinal surface of right lung
seeds.label: The mediastinal surfaces of the two lungs carry different impressions: the right is grooved by the SVC and azygos arch, the left by the aortic arch and its two great branches
seeds.definition: On the right lung's mediastinal surface, in front of and above the hilum lie the cardiac impression (related to the right atrium and auricle), the superior vena caval groove, the impression for the ascending aorta, the inferior vena caval groove, the groove for the arch of the azygos vein, and the tracheal and oesophageal grooves, the latter continuing behind the hilum.
seeds.objective: Name the vascular and visceral impressions on the mediastinal surface of the right lung, in front of, above and behind the hilum.
seeds.pitfall: Placing the ascending aorta's impression on the left lung — it belongs to the right lung, anterior to the hilum.
seeds.subject: resp

seeds.asked: describe the inerior of Rt. atrium
seeds.label: The right atrium is split by the crista terminalis into a rough atrium proper and a smooth sinus venarum; the right ventricle has an inflow part with three papillary muscles and a smooth infundibulum
seeds.definition: The right atrium's cavity is divided by the crista terminalis, a muscular ridge between the openings of the superior and inferior venae cavae, into an anterior rough atrium proper, roughened by the musculi pectinati, and a posterior smooth sinus venarum, which receives the superior vena cava (no valve), the inferior vena cava (a rudimentary valve) and the coronary sinus (a small valve). Its septal wall carries the fossa ovalis and its raised margin, the annulus ovalis, deficient below.
seeds.objective: Describe the interior of the right atrium: the crista terminalis, atrium proper, sinus venarum and septal wall features.
seeds.pitfall: Forgetting the valve state of each opening into the sinus venarum — the SVC has none, the IVC and coronary sinus each have a rudimentary one.
seeds.subject: cvs

seeds.asked: compare Rt. coronary and Lt. coronary regarding origin and distribution
seeds.label: The right coronary artery runs the coronary sulcus to give the marginal and posterior interventricular arteries, supplying the whole right side of the heart and, in most people, the whole conducting system
seeds.definition: The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus. It supplies the whole right atrium, the whole right ventricle except a strip beside the anterior interventricular groove, a strip of the left ventricle's diaphragmatic surface, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, and the conducting system in most people: the SA node in 60% and the AV node and bundle branches in 80%.
seeds.objective: State the origin and distribution of the right coronary artery, for comparison against the left.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming the right coronary artery always supplies the SA node — only 60% of people.
seeds.subject: cvs

seeds.asked: compare Rt. coronary and Lt. coronary regarding origin and distribution (left coronary side)
seeds.label: The left coronary artery divides into the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, together supplying the left atrium, most of the left ventricle and the anterior two thirds of the septum
seeds.definition: The left coronary artery, larger than the right, arises from the left posterior aortic sinus and divides into the anterior interventricular artery — supplying the sternocostal surface of the left ventricle, a strip of the right ventricle and the anterior two thirds of the septum — and the circumflex artery — supplying the left atrium and, via its marginal branch, the left ventricle down to the apex, and the SA node in 40% and AV node in 20% of people.
seeds.objective: State the origin and distribution of the left coronary artery, for comparison against the right.
seeds.pitfall: Crediting the anterior interventricular artery with the posterior third of the septum — that belongs to the right coronary artery.

seeds.asked: enumerate the structures found in lower concave aspect of arch of aorta
seeds.label: The arch of the aorta passes over the left bronchus and gives the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries from its convexity, with the trachea and oesophagus behind it
seeds.definition: The arch of the aorta's lower concave aspect overlies the pulmonary trunk's bifurcation, the left principal bronchus, the ligamentum arteriosum, the superficial cardiac plexus and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
seeds.objective: List the five structures related to the lower concave aspect of the aortic arch.
seeds.pitfall: Placing the deep cardiac plexus on the arch's concavity — it sits on the arch's right posterior aspect at the tracheal bifurcation; the superficial plexus is the one on the concavity.

seeds.asked: Rt. phrenic nerve, origin, course and branches
seeds.label: The phrenic nerve enters the thorax on the venous side (right) or arterial side (left) of the mediastinum and leaves through the diaphragm it alone supplies motor to
seeds.definition: The right phrenic nerve enters the thorax through the thoracic inlet in front of the subclavian artery and behind the start of the brachiocephalic vein, crosses the internal thoracic artery, and descends in front of the lung root, running down the right side of the right brachiocephalic vein, the SVC, the pericardium over the right atrium and the IVC, leaving through the vena caval opening on the IVC's right. It supplies the whole of the diaphragm's motor innervation on its side, and pericardial and diaphragmatic-pleura sensory branches.
seeds.objective: Give the origin, thoracic course and branches of the right phrenic nerve.
seeds.pitfall: Assigning the phrenic nerve's course by symmetry — the right and left differ in their mediastinal relations and site of exit through the diaphragm.

seeds.label: The Na+-K+ ATPase, the Ca++-ATPase and the Na+-Ca++ exchanger maintain cardiac myocyte ionic gradients, and the exchanger can reverse direction
seeds.definition: Every action potential lets Na+ and Ca++ leak into the cardiac myocyte and K+ leak out. Three sarcolemmal transport proteins correct this and so maintain the resting membrane potential's underlying gradients: the Na+-K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in (electrogenic); a separate Ca++-ATPase pumps Ca++ out; and the Na+-Ca++ exchanger normally exchanges 3 Na+ in for 1 Ca++ out, though it can reverse when intracellular Na+ rises.
seeds.objective: Name the three sarcolemmal transporters that restore cardiac ionic gradients and maintain the resting membrane potential, with the Na+-K+ ATPase's stoichiometry.
seeds.pitfall: Treating the Na+-Ca++ exchanger's direction as fixed — it reverses when intracellular Na+ rises, e.g. with digitalis.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Electrical Activity of the Heart

seeds.label: Beta-adrenergic stimulation raises cytoplasmic calcium through Protein Kinase A to increase both contractile force (positive inotropy) and the speed of relaxation (lusitropy), while hypoxia and ischaemia impair both
seeds.definition: Beta-adrenergic stimulation (sympathetic nerves or circulating catecholamines) raises cAMP and activates PKA, which phosphorylates the L-type Ca++ channel (more Ca++ entry) and the ryanodine receptor (more Ca++ release from the SR) — a positive inotropic effect — and phosphorylates phospholamban to speed SERCA reuptake, a positive lusitropic effect. Negative inotropy follows from impaired ATP supply: hypoxia and myocardial ischaemia both reduce contractile force and slow relaxation.
seeds.objective: Explain the cAMP-PKA mechanism of positive inotropy and lusitropy, and give causes of negative inotropy.
seeds.pitfall: Treating inotropy and lusitropy as unrelated — the same PKA activation drives both, through different phosphorylation targets.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Mechanical Properties of Cardiac Muscle

seeds.asked: define cardiac output, mention factors increase, decrease it
seeds.label: Cardiac output is the volume each ventricle pumps per minute, equals heart rate times stroke volume, and is corrected for body size as the cardiac index
seeds.definition: Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute, normally about 5 litres/minute, equal to stroke volume x heart rate. CO increases with physical exercise (up to 700%), anxiety and excitement (up to 100%), after meals (30%), high environmental temperature, and pregnancy; it decreases with standing up from supine (30%) and with rapid cardiac arrhythmias and many other heart diseases.
seeds.objective: Define cardiac output and its formula, and list conditions that increase and decrease it.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming any tachyarrhythmia raises cardiac output — the book places rapid arrhythmias among the causes of decreased CO.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Cardiac Function

seeds.asked: compare APC and PNC regarding site, nature, send, receive, importance
seeds.label: The dorsal respiratory group drives normal quiet breathing alone, the ventral respiratory group activates only for forced breathing, and the pontine apneustic and pneumotaxic centres tune the medullary rhythm rather than generating it
seeds.definition: The apneustic centre (APC) sits in the lower pons, is made of tonically-discharging inspiratory neurons, receives inhibitory input from the pneumotaxic centre (PNC) and lung stretch receptors, and sends tonic excitatory (inspiratory) signals to the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) — its unopposed activity, if disconnected from the PNC and vagus, causes apneustic breathing (prolonged gasping inspiration). The pneumotaxic centre (PNC) sits in the upper pons, is made of inhibitory neurons, receives stimulation from the DRG, and sends inhibitory signals to the DRG and APC — switching off inspiration and starting expiration, so tuning the rate and depth of breathing.
seeds.objective: Compare the apneustic and pneumotaxic centres by site, the nature of their neurons, their afferent and efferent connections, and their importance to the respiratory rhythm.
seeds.pitfall: Crediting the pontine centres with generating the basic respiratory rhythm — that is the medullary pre-Botzinger complex and DRG's job; the pons only tunes it.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Respiratory System > Control of Respiration

P5.prompt: Regulation of arteriolar diameter — mention factors determining it (5 that constrict and 5 that dilate)
expects: Myogenic autoregulation: a rise in perfusion pressure stretches arteriolar smooth muscle, raising Ca++ entry and causing vasoconstriction; a fall in pressure has the opposite effect (vasodilatation) [Physiology dept book p. 63]

Metabolic autoregulation: a fall in flow causes hypoxia and accumulation of vasodilator metabolites, relaxing the arterioles; conversely raised flow/metabolism has the opposite (constrictor) tendency [Physiology dept book p. 63]

Endothelial factors: nitric oxide (from shear stress, acetylcholine, bradykinin, histamine) is a vasodilator; endothelin is not documented in the extracted text this run [Physiology dept book p. 65-66]
Humoral vasoconstrictors: angiotensin II, epinephrine (at high levels), norepinephrine, vasopressin [Physiology dept book p. 69]
Humoral vasodilators: kinins, natriuretic peptide; epinephrine at physiological levels is net-dilator in skeletal muscle/liver via beta2 receptors [Physiology dept book p. 69]
Nervous control: decreased tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor discharge produces vasodilatation in most tissues [Physiology dept book p. 69]

P6.prompt: Compare anemic hypoxia and stagnant hypoxia regarding arterial PO2, O2 content, O2 saturation %, venous PO2, O2 content, O2 saturation %, and cyanosis
expects: Anemic hypoxia: arterial PO2 and % saturation are normal (ventilation/gas exchange unaffected); arterial O2 content is reduced (less Hb to carry O2); venous O2 content and PO2 are further reduced because tissues extract extra O2 from each unit of the reduced-Hb blood [Physiology dept book pp. 154-155]

Stagnant hypoxia: blood flow through capillaries is very slow, so tissues withdraw extra O2 from each unit of capillary blood, giving reduced PO2 and O2 content in venous blood; arterial values are not stated as abnormal in the book's prose [Physiology dept book p. 158]

Cyanosis: does NOT appear with anemic hypoxia (total Hb, oxygenated and deoxygenated, is reduced); DOES appear with stagnant hypoxia (low flow lets tissues strip extra O2 from each unit of Hb, raising reduced Hb locally) [Physiology dept book pp. 159-160]
